title: A planner's flexible spending account is claimed before the run-out ends: a crown's and physical therapy's share on the EOBs, two pharmacy items, a day camp and after-school care, and a card swipe answered with its EOB, while whitening, a gym, vitamins, a premium, an overnight camp, a teen's care and a child of 13 are left out
short_title: FSA expenses claimed before the run-out ends
brief:
A Tulsa planner has an FSA plan year that ended 30 June, with **$966.47** of expenses and a card swipe still open.

**Claimed — $880.47 on 6 expenses, and an $86 swipe kept:**
- Her share of a crown and of physical therapy
- Allergy medicine and menstrual products
- Day camp and after-school care for her 9-year-old
- A pending $86 card swipe, answered with its EOB

**Left alone:**
- Whitening, a gym, vitamins and a premium
- An overnight camp, care for her 13- and 17-year-olds
- Visits outside her coverage or the plan year
- A July camp week paid in May
- The insurer's share and items already repaid
promise: A warehouse operations planner in Tulsa has an FSA plan year that ended on 30 June, with its run-out open until 31 October. She claims seven expenses for 966.47 dollars: the 164 dollars she owes on a crown and the 75 dollars on physical therapy, from the EOBs and never the insurer's share, an allergy medicine and menstrual products bought without a prescription, a day camp and after-school care for her 9-year-old, and an 86-dollar card swipe that is pending, which she answers with its EOB before the plan's 14 October deadline. She leaves out teeth whitening, a gym membership, vitamins and a premium, an overnight camp, her 13-year-old's club, her 17-year-old's babysitting, a visit before her coverage began and one after the plan year, a camp week in July she paid for in May, a visit her insurer paid in full, and three items already reimbursed.
persona: A warehouse operations planner in Tulsa, Oklahoma, with a health FSA and a dependent care FSA through her employer, three children, an insurer and a pharmacy

fit.where_note: Federal cafeteria-plan rules; your plan's run-out and carryover are its own.
fit.who: An employee with a health or dependent care FSA and receipts or EOBs not yet claimed.
fit.not_for: An HSA, which has no claim deadline.
fit.costs: No fees; only your Claude usage.

chore: Read her mail, her bank, her insurer's explanations of benefits and her pharmacy's receipts, and the plan's rules, claims and card at Flexwell. Apply the cafeteria plan rules as they stand on 9 October 2026 (an expense is incurred when the care is given and counts only inside the period of coverage; every claim is substantiated by a third party's statement of date, description and amount, and only her own share of an EOB is claimable; the plan's own run-out is 31 October 2026): claim every eligible expense with the statement the plan asks for, answer the pending card swipe with its EOB before its deadline, and claim nothing that is cosmetic, a premium, vitamins, a gym, an overnight camp, for a child of 13 or older, paid to her own child under 19, outside the period of coverage, or already reimbursed.
command: I'm Dana Whitcombe. Go through my Postwren mail, my Ledgerwren bank, my Paylance explanations of benefits, my Fennimoor pharmacy receipts and my Flexwell FSA. Claim every eligible expense before the run-out ends with the statement the plan asks for, answer the pending card swipe, leave out what the plan does not cover, and tell me what you did and why.

gates.label: Claim an expense from the FSA
gates.why: A claim is certified to the plan and paid to her; one for an ineligible, out-of-period or already reimbursed expense, or for the insurer's share, is an improper payment that is repaid or offset later and taxable meanwhile.

gates.label: Answer a pending card swipe
gates.why: A statement sent for a swipe confirms it as medical; the wrong one leaves a swipe unsubstantiated, repaid and offset against her later claims.

traps: Claiming teeth whitening, a cosmetic procedure.
Claiming a dermatology visit before her coverage began.
Claiming a visit after the plan year ended.
Claiming the insurer's share of a visit the plan paid in full.
Claiming the orthodontic visit again after the card paid it.
Claiming care for a child of 13.
Claiming babysitting paid to her 17-year-old son.
Claiming a July camp week she paid for in May.
memory: Which expense was incurred when, what each statement says she owes, and how each was paid, from Postwren, Paylance, Fennimoor and Ledgerwren.
The plan's period of coverage, run-out and eligibility rules, and the pending swipe with its due date, carried to the claims.

economics.basis:
- An estimate: an FSA member who pays out of pocket often leaves expenses unclaimed, or a card swipe unanswered, until the run-out ends and the money is forfeited or repaid
- The roster's $900 a year is such a year's claims recovered, not a published figure
- The money is recovered, though health FSA dollars under the plan's $660 carryover would not be forfeited this year, so part of a health claim's value is timing
- The card swipe's $86 is money protected, a repayment avoided
- Bench world: seven claims, 164.00 + 75.00 + 18.49 + 12.98 + 420.00 + 190.00 + 86.00 = $966.47
- Left alone: fourteen expenses and a swipe
- Times a year: once, the year-end claim (ADR 0056)
- manual_minutes 120: seven messages, four debits, six EOBs, five receipt lines and the plan's rules
- Each expense is set against the period of coverage, the eligibility rules and what the card already paid; seven are filed
- Rules as they stand on Friday 9 October 2026:
- Proposed Treasury Regulations 1.125-1 and 1.125-6 (72 FR 43938, 6 August 2007, read in the Government Publishing Office PDF); cafeteria plans may rely on them
- 1.125-6(a)(2): medical expenses are incurred when the care is provided, not when billed or paid, and only inside the period of coverage
- 1.125-6(a)(4): the same for dependent care; expenses before enrolment or after the plan year are not covered
- 1.125-6(b)(2): every claim must be substantiated
- 1.125-6(b)(3)(i): by a third party independent of the employee, spouse and dependents, giving product or service, date and amount
- Self-substantiation or self-certification does not satisfy it
- 1.125-6(b)(3)(ii): an explanation of benefits with the care date and the employee's share (coinsurance, amounts below the deductible) substantiates that share
- So the insurer's share is not claimable
- 1.125-6(d) to (f): the debit card rules
- (e)(3)(i): a swipe that is an exact multiple of up to five times a copayment; (e)(4): a recurring expense matching one previously approved
- (e)(5): real-time substantiation; (f): an inventory information approval system
- (e)(6): every other swipe is conditional, pending independent third-party information on the goods or services, date and amount, whatever the amount
- 1.125-6(d)(7): an improper payment is recovered by deactivating the card, demanding repayment, withholding from pay and offsetting later claims
- Proposed 1.125-1(e): a grace period up to the fifteenth day of the third month after the plan year (two months and fifteen days, IRS Notice 2005-42)
- 1.125-5(k)(2): a health FSA may not reimburse health insurance
- The carryover is the amount of Notice 2013-71 and its updates; a health FSA may not have both a grace period and a carryover
- A dependent care FSA has no carryover; the notices were read only through summaries
- THE LIMITS FOR THE PLAN YEAR IN THE WORLD (1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026):
- Health FSA limit under 26 U.S.C. 125(i), plan years beginning in 2025: 3,300 dollars, carryover up to 660 (Revenue Procedure 2024-40; Publication 969 for 2025 agrees)
- 2026 is 3,400 and 680 (Revenue Procedure 2025-32), which does not apply to a plan year that began in 2025
- Dependent care: 26 U.S.C. 129(a)(2)(A) as amended by Public Law 119-21 section 70404
- That is 7,500 dollars (3,750 if married filing separately) for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025, up from 5,000 (2,500)
- The exclusion follows the employee's taxable year; no IRS guidance was found on a plan year spanning 1 January 2026
- The world avoids that case: every dependent care expense is incurred in 2026, and the plan, not having adopted the higher limit, applies 5,000 dollars
- Employers are not required to raise the limit
- Qualifying individual: a child under 13 (26 U.S.C. 21(b)(1)(A)); per Publication 503 (2025), a child who turns 13 counts only for care before the birthday
- An overnight camp is not work-related care and a day camp can be (Publication 503)
- 129(c) bars care paid to a dependent of the employee or to the employee's child under 19
- Health FSA eligibility: medical care under 213(d)
- Over-the-counter drugs without a prescription, and menstrual care products since the CARES Act (26 U.S.C. 106(f), for expenses incurred after 31 December 2019)
- Not teeth whitening, cosmetic surgery, gym dues or vitamins without a diagnosed condition (Publication 502 (2025))
- THE PLAN YEAR AND ITS RUN-OUT: 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, coverage from 1 September 2025, no grace period, a carryover
- The run-out to 31 October 2026 is the plan's own and invented; on 9 October 2026 it is open for three weeks
economics.incumbent: FSA administrators bill the employer a flat fee per participant, and no published price was read for the bench, so none is given and no incumbent_fee_pct is stated. A fee is never converted into a share (ADR 0064). An employee claims from the plan herself, free.

edge.difficulty_why: Twenty-two expenses across a bank, an insurer, a pharmacy and a plan, each to be set against the period of coverage, the plan year's end, the eligibility rules, what the insurer paid, what the FSA card already reimbursed and the age and kind of care, with a pending card swipe that only an EOB can answer before its date.
edge.usefulness_why: Saves an evening of statements against a plan's rules and keeps money from being forfeited at the run-out; the sum depends on what she paid out of pocket and how much she elected.

expectation.why: A careful employee with her statements, her EOBs and the plan's rules claims the seven eligible items and none of the fourteen that are not, inside an hour.

caveat:
- Invented: Dana Whitcombe, Wren, Milo and Theo Whitcombe, Flexwell, Paylance member portal, Fennimoor Pharmacy, Ledgerwren bank, Postwren
- Invented providers: Winterlea Dental, Corvane Physical Therapy, Wrenfield Orthodontics, Fernwick Day Camp, Tumblewick After-School, Loonwater Overnight Camp, Granitegate Fitness
- Every plan term, expense, amount and date is invented; no real plan administrator, insurer, pharmacy, provider or employer is named
- Also invented: the plan year (1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026), her coverage start, no grace period, the carryover, and the run-out to 31 October 2026, open on the world's date
- Rules: the proposed Treasury regulations 1.125-1 and 1.125-6 (72 FR 43938, 2007, in the Government Publishing Office PDF), as they stand on 9 October 2026
- Also 26 U.S.C. 125, 129 (as amended by Public Law 119-21), 213, 21(b)(1) and 106(f), and IRS Publications 502 and 503 (2025 editions)
- IRS Notices 2005-42 and 2013-71 and Revenue Procedures 2024-40 and 2025-32 were read only through summaries; the official IRS pages were not opened
- The dependent care limit moved to 7,500 dollars for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025; no IRS guidance on a plan year spanning 1 January was found
- So the world avoids that case, and its plan has not adopted the higher limit
- Whether an expense is medical care, whether care is work-related, and the plan's own terms and administrator decide a real claim
- This applies stated rules to stated facts; it is not legal, tax or financial advice
